summary: We built Gale et al. to help crews choose when and how to travel across Gale Crater on a pressurized rover. Users pick both a start point and an end point. The planner uses terrain data, temperature and radiation levels at the surface to find a route that balances travel time and radiation exposure while trying to minimise harm on the crew.
details:
Gale et al. is an interactive route planner for exploring Gale Crater on Mars. We started with a practical question: if a crew needs to get from A to B, how should the route change depending on when they leave and whether they travel on foot or by rover?

The crew selects two points on the map, a travel mode and a departure time in local Martian solar time. Our routing engine uses A* search to evaluate possible paths across a HiRISE digital elevation model. It considers slope, surface roughness, temperature and radiation exposure. The radiation model accounts for how much of the sky is visible from each location, so surrounding terrain can provide some shielding. For each route, the planner estimates travel time, elevation gain and accumulated radiation dose. A marker follows the route using the calculated arrival time at each waypoint.

One feature we wanted was the ability to explore a decision before committing to it. A user can move the time slider, see how modeled conditions change across the same terrain, and calculate the journey again. We also built a simulator for dust storms and solar particle events. It lets us demonstrate how the crew would receive a warning during a traverse. Our next step is to use those alerts to recalculate the remaining route from the crew’s current position and minimize exposure to the event.

We prepared the terrain layers in QGIS, wrote the routing and environmental models in C, and connected them to the map through a Python Flask API. The interface uses JavaScript, OpenLayers and Vite. We chose a default routing step of 20 meters to keep planning interactive, with a 1-meter option for finer calculations. The intended impact is to make mission-planning trade-offs visible: a crew can see where a detour adds travel time, avoids a steep slope or reduces its estimated radiation dose.
